analysis.one_liner: Lets workers refuse forced arbitration in job disputes and bans making it a condition of employment.
analysis.headline: The bill to let workers choose or refuse arbitration in job disputes never got a hearing or vote; it died in a House Judiciary subcommittee after two years.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Federal Arbitration Act so that an employer could not use a contract clause to force an employee into arbitration over a job dispute. Arbitration would only happen if, after a dispute actually arises, one side asks in writing and the other agrees within 60 days. It would also bar employers from making workers sign away their right to sue as a condition of getting or keeping a job.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who sign employment contracts containing arbitration clauses. Today those clauses usually require them to bring discrimination, harassment, wage, and firing claims before a private arbitrator instead of a judge and jury, with closed proceedings and no appeal. The bill would let them wait until a dispute happens and then choose to go to court or agree to arbitration.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employees with arbitration clauses in contracts

how_it_helps.text: Arbitration over a workplace dispute could proceed only if, after the dispute arises, one party requests it in writing and the other consents within 60 days — so a clause signed at hire could not decide the forum years later.
Employers would be barred from requiring an employee to arbitrate a dispute as a condition of employment.
The change would apply only to contracts entered into or renewed after enactment, leaving existing clauses unchanged.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would lose the contractual power to channel employee claims — discrimination, harassment, wage, and firing cases — into a private forum without juries, public records, or appeal. Arbitration providers, who sell that forum, would lose a large stream of mandatory cases.

drawbacks.text: Arbitration is faster and cheaper than court for both sides in many cases; some workers with small-dollar claims might find a courtroom less accessible than an arbitrator, and employer groups have long argued mandatory arbitration can resolve disputes more efficiently.
The bill applies only to contracts signed or renewed after enactment, so millions of workers already bound by arbitration clauses would get no relief.
The bill drew no cosponsors, suggesting other lawmakers saw problems with the approach even beyond simple lack of support.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers with arbitration clauses, the upside — keeping the option of a court, a jury, and a public record for serious claims like discrimination and harassment — is substantial and the direct cost is small, since arbitration by mutual agreement would still be available. The main honest objection is efficiency: arbitration can be cheaper and quicker, and this bill would not help anyone already stuck under an existing clause. On balance the benefits to workers outweigh the efficiency costs, though the bill was never seriously pursued.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee two days after introduction and forwarded to a subcommittee a month later; no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews introduced the bill on February 5, 2003.
The House referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
On March 6, 2003, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, where it sat for the rest of the Congress.
No further action is recorded through the end of the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that write mandatory arbitration clauses into employment contracts keep their power to steer workplace disputes away from court, and the arbitration industry keeps its supply of mandatory cases. Workers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers with arbitration clauses, arbitration providers

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter of record.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred and never scheduled
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill, sending it to a subcommittee where it died without action.

against.name: House Republicans
against.role: Majority party controlling the House and its committee agendas, 2003-2005
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House and Judiciary Committee during the 108th Congress and set the agenda under which the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken. The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and no recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and the private dispute-resolution industry
industries.note: Mandatory employment arbitration clauses feed a steady stream of cases to private arbitration firms and arbitrators. The bill would have made those cases voluntary, cutting off the guaranteed demand.

Employers use arbitration clauses to keep discrimination, harassment, and wage claims out of court before juries and out of the public record. The bill would have stripped that power for new and renewed contracts.
